subjects.displayTitle: Defending the Faith: evidence, courtesy, and the care of a community
subjects.introduction: Two accused men were freed because someone at a consulate compared a handwriting, a signature and a seal, and found the letter against them forged. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts this with gratitude, and the episode holds in miniature what defending the Faith involves: evidence patiently examined, people protected, and the truth allowed to speak for itself. Bahá’u’lláh makes every believer, according to ability, a refuter of attacks on the Cause, but by pen and tongue, never by sword or violence, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that the language must be moderate, tempered and infinitely courteous, whatever tone the opponent chose. A sincere doubt deserves an answer rather than a rebuke, and a believer’s conduct is read by others as the conduct of the religion itself. Beside these principles stand urgent instructions from times of danger, which belong to their circumstances. The First Epistle of Peter joins readiness to give a reason for one’s hope with meekness and a good conscience, so that the manner of an answer becomes part of its evidence [1]. From here the path leads into wisdom in speech and action, the firmness of the Covenant against those who would breach it, and the careful review of what is published in the Faith’s name.
subjects.arc: Begin with verified evidence and courteous language, explore reasoned and collaborative answers, then examine protection in historical settings before closing with impartial conduct.

order.why: Make the pen and tongue, rather than violence, the stated means of defense.
shortened: It is incumbent upon all men, each according to his ability, to refute the arguments of those that have attacked the Faith of God.
He that wisheth to promote the Cause of the one true God, let him promote it through his pen and tongue, rather than have recourse to sword or violence.

If any man were to arise to defend, in his writings, the Cause of God against its assailants, such a man, however inconsiderable his share, shall be so honored in the world to come that the Concourse on high would envy his glory.

order.why: Open with the concrete investigation that identified a forged letter and freed the accused.
Establish moderate and courteous language as an explicit standard.
Read the invitation to express doubts and receive an answer within its polemical setting.
shortened: However, in truth, if a soul were to be found who harbored doubts due to the intimations of the ungodly, it would surely be appreciated were he to mention his doubts, for we in this land have no occupation and stand ready, should anyone experience any doubt, to provide an answer according to our station and capacity and his station, that perchance through divine grace his heart might be sanctified from vain imaginings and empty suppositions.

order.why: Read the reported distinction between proofs and calumny.
shortened: Our methods are different, we do not attack, neither calumniate; we do not wish to dispute with them; we bring forth proofs and arguments; we invite them to confute our statements. They cannot answer us, but instead, they write all they can think of against the Divine Messenger, Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Consider how conduct is attributed to the religion one represents.
shortened: Say: Beware, O people, lest ye commit that which would dishonor the Cause of your Lord, the Mighty, the Loving, for whatsoever ye commit, the people attribute to the Source of the Cause, as ye yourselves witness.

order.why: Explore defense as protection of a population as well as observance.
Center the safety of people who are known by the name of the Faith.
Read the remembered protection of friends in danger.
Consider the stated reasons for declining confrontation with an author.
shortened: First, it is not permissible for this servant to engage in confrontation with such persons, as it would cause rebellion and cut off hope and lead to despair in that author.

order.why: Read kindness and non-interference alongside confidence that hostile publications will not harm the Cause.
shortened: The previous publications caused no harm to the Cause of God, and I hope that, on the contrary, they will yield positive results. We harbor no ill feelings toward him; rather, we have guided all to kindness and non-interference. Even now, whatever he may write in his new book will cause us no harm, though it may ultimately lead to his own regret.

order.why: Explore a study group’s preparation of answers as an opportunity for learning.
Read the call to pool knowledge in a specific historical dispute.
Consider the practical work of recording alterations and explaining them to seekers.
Keep the historical refuge given to the Bab distinct from the narrated argument about proof and tradition.
shortened: But the Babi chiefs composed treatises against them, and set in order replies according to their own thought. Were these to be discussed in detail it would conduce to prolixity, and our object is the statement of history, not of arguments for believing or rejecting; but of some of the replies the gist is this: that they held the Proof as supreme, and the evidence as outweighing traditions, considering the former as the root and the latter as the branch, and saying, "If the branch agree not with the root it serves not as an argument and is unworthy of reliance; for the reported consequence has no right to oppose itself to the established principle, and cannot argue against it."

order.why: Read the account of answering difficult questions in Iraq as a testimony within the source.
shortened: O thou who gazest upon the Kingdom of God! In the days when the Ancient Beauty and the Most Great Name illumined the horizon of Iraq with the lights of His dawning, all the leaders of the peoples - whether scholars, men of learning, princes or nobles - would present themselves in His holy court and verbally pose their most difficult and complex questions. These would be answered immediately from His pure lips with the most wondrous utterance and perfect exposition. They would then depart in complete contentment, acknowledgment and recognition of the all-encompassing power of the All-Merciful.

order.why: Keep the reported recollection of reasoning with scholars in its own voice.
Read the account of discussion grounded in proofs and evidence.
Hear the pleasure expressed at a particular gathering with divines.
Consider the defense of earlier Prophets across religious boundaries.
shortened: All opponents know that we prove Christ's Prophethood to the Jews with proofs and evidences, establish the universal Prophethood of Muhammad to the Christians with rational, traditional and conclusive proofs, and demonstrate to the Zoroastrians with clear evidence the Prophethood of all Prophets and Messengers from Adam to the Seal, sacrificing our lives in the path of the Prophets and crying out under the sword.

order.why: Keep the reported defense of Muhammad against missionary writings attributed.
Read the report’s claims about the spread of the Bible as historical argument, not editorially verified history.
Consider the reported wish to dispel misunderstandings about learning and philosophy.
Read the reported value assigned to logical, intellectual, and spiritual arguments.
shortened: In this day, the most useful books are those which demonstrate the validity of the Cause with logical proofs, intellectual evidences and spiritual arguments.

order.why: Consider the report’s explanation of occasions when speaking is needed.
Hear the permission to compose a complete response to a particular book.
Keep the instruction concerning Wilson’s book in its historical setting.
Read the hope that capable writers will arise.
shortened: This servant's hope is that in those regions, in a short time, souls will arise who will compose treatises and writings proving the Cause of God with utmost eloquence and fluency and the ultimate power and might.

order.why: Consider encouragement for useful writing and the promise of later reading.
Hear the prayerful appreciation of a written refutation.
shortened: When, O my God, I had taken my station facing the Spot around which circle those that are nigh unto Thee, lo, there was before me a written letter, a guarded tablet, and an outspread roll containing cogent proofs, clear testimonies and lucid evidences in refutation of one who had striven to repudiate Thy truth.

order.why: Read the reported sequence of criticism and Abu’l-Fadl’s response.
shortened: The sheikh of Islam, of Caucasia, wrote against the Cause. Some of the friends answered him. Sheikh of Islam wrote a second time a criticism. After that, Agha Mirza Abul-Fazl wrote a full, convincing answer. It surprised the sheikh.

order.why: Consider study and reflection on a particular treatise as preparation.
shortened: His Honor Mirza Abu'l-Fadl has written a treatise answering the criticisms of a London preacher. Each one of you should have a copy.[1] Read, memorize and reflect upon it. Then, when accusations and criticisms are advanced by those unfavorable to the Cause, you will be well armed.

order.why: Keep the assignment of a response to Abu’l-Fadl as a specific account.
Read the prayer for Abu’l-Fadl alongside its explicit means of evidence and exposition.
shortened: O Lord! Verily Thy servant Abu'l-Fadl hath arisen to aid Thy Cause, to silence Thy opponents, to compel Thy disputants, and to break the power of those who war against Thee, by spreading proofs and presenting decisive evidence with clear exposition, refuting the doubts of the party of falsehood who are committed to sophistry and concealment so as to make the matter unclear to those weak in mind and heart.

order.why: Keep the related prayer’s forceful language within its devotional purpose.
shortened: O God! Assist Your servant Abu'l-Fada'il to prove Your religion, proclaim Your proof, clarify Your evidence, exalt Your Word, repel Your opponents, turn back Your adversaries, silence Your enemies, and confound those who dispute against the Truth.

order.why: Attribute the polemical metaphors to the source while noticing the requested clear exposition.
Read the priority given to the particular reply to Browne.
Keep the allegations concerning a disputed history attributed to the Tablet.
Consider the source’s allegations of alteration and its direction to consult available writings.
shortened: Half of this person's book consists of fabrications and he has altered and changed many words. Soon he will find himself in manifest loss.

In Azerbaijan, with perfect wisdom spread word that this person's writings were purely intended as slander. If you want the truth of this matter, the books and treatises of proofs are available - observe that none of these fabrications are mentioned in them.

order.why: Read the account of hostile publication and feared violence in its local historical setting.
Retain the reported accusation as an accusation being answered, not an editorial fact.
Consider the use of an opponent’s published letter as evidence for reform and reconciliation.
Read the particular permission to publish letters clarifying misrepresentations.
Keep the specific limits on showing and distributing a response.
shortened: A response was written and sent to be published and distributed. Show it to some of the impartial members of the assembly but do not give them copies.

order.why: Connect careful communication with authorities to the fear of provoking wider alarm.
shortened: Whenever appropriate, they should explain to the Ambassador what the Blessed Beauty, may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones, has said about obedience to kings and loyalty and goodwill toward crowned rulers, especially the prayers He has offered for His Majesty the Sultan and His Majesty the Shah of Iran, so that the truth of the matter becomes clear and evident to the authorities. For enemies both familiar and foreign have risen and will continue to rise with endless calumnies and accusations to completely obscure the truth of the matter.

As previously mentioned, you should accomplish your task step by step with utmost caution, care and calm, lest this matter should create alarm and perturbation in the hearts of the people who, being ignorant of the actual facts, would conceive the idea of a large organisation.

order.why: Read the denial of accusations alongside counsel concerning government loyalty.
shortened: When these Yahyayi Babis, who are the enemies of the Baha'is, commit any shameful act, they accuse the Baha'is, and the ill-wishers cry out that all are corrupt. But the truth will not remain hidden - it must surely become evident and manifest.
Therefore do not tremble at these calumnies, but rather follow the sacred texts by obeying the government and serving His Imperial Majesty with the utmost sincerity and trustworthiness.

order.why: Keep the limited private gatherings within the circumstances described.
shortened: When these are firmly established, private assemblies shall be abolished. However, since public gatherings cannot at present be established in various lands, as they would cause the agitation of the wicked and the interference of the ungodly, there is no objection to establishing private gatherings wherein the number of those present corresponds to the sacred number of the Greatest Name. The purpose of this is to prevent large crowds from gathering, which would cause alarm, distress and the lamentation of the ignorant.

order.why: Read the explanation of the nine-by-nine arrangement and fear of suspicion.
shortened: The purpose of the "nine by nine" at the time of Mirza Tarazu'llah's arrival was that the friends should not gather in large numbers in one place, for the ill-wishers are extremely hostile and lying in wait. As soon as they see several people together, they become suspicious and resort to slander.

order.why: Consider the warning that disclosure could endanger the Holy Land.
Keep concealment under tyranny tied to the stated protection of people.
shortened: None should acknowledge that which he possesseth, for the protection of those who have turned towards the Countenance - a command from the presence of One mighty and powerful.

O concourse of loved ones! Conceal the pearls of divine knowledge from the eyes of the treacherous ones. None should acknowledge the Cause of God before the faces of those through whose tyranny the dwellers of the Most Exalted Paradise did lament, and every perceiving mystic did cry out.

order.why: Read the historical letter-of-introduction requirement in its context of feared infiltration.
shortened: Any Iranian or non-Iranian person who comes from the East without having a letter from me bearing my signature, even if they are among my relatives, the friends must absolutely not accept them nor allow them into their gatherings. For wolves will come from Iran to those regions to tear apart the divine sheep and cause corruption and discord, especially those associated with Mirza Yahya.

order.why: Retain the parallel instruction concerning documentation as a particular historical direction.
shortened: You must protect the Cause of God and write to everyone and awaken them that they must absolutely not meet with any Iranian person without a document from me in their hand with my writing and signature.

order.why: Notice that the historical restriction explicitly included the writer’s own grandsons.
Keep the related requirement for a handwritten and sealed letter distinct.
Read the warning about visitors sent to create doubt within its setting.
shortened: Because some sects will send certain men to mingle with you in order to throw suspicion upon those who are weak, therefore avoid them carefully.

order.why: Attribute the reported characterization of infiltrators to the source.
shortened: But the friends must be aware and alert, and eschew the company of such masters of deceit, and if they see someone who has supporters and followers, they must exercise great care and find out what plans are in his heart and what ambitions motivate his mind, since these people have no motive but to infiltrate the Faith.

order.why: Examine the reported distinction between freedom of conscience and undermining a shared institution.
shortened: Would I not be responsible to Baha'u'llah if I stand aloof and do not stop the man who with an axe in his hand is trying to undermine the foundation of the religion of God? Should I utter no word and approve his destructive work? I am not interfering with the dictates of his conscience. I simply say if he desires to be a laborer in this edifice he must build and not destroy.

order.why: Keep the judgment about harmful conduct in its particular disciplinary setting.
Read the conditional warning based on what the recipient had reported.
Consider the specific concern for members of the family and their protection.
shortened: You must exercise the utmost protection regarding others, especially the leaves of the blessed tree, lest anyone cast doubts and misgivings upon them verbally or in writing.

order.why: Read preparation for possible disorder in the Holy Land.
Consider personal travel, kindness, and reasoned answers as proposed assistance.
Hear the responsibilities addressed to an assembly.
shortened: O ye members of the shining assembly! Each one of you must resist doubts (or false rumors) in those parts like unto a great barrier, until the invisible confirmations may appear and merciful assistance may become manifest.

order.why: Read the power of proof as the stated means of dispelling doubts.
shortened: The friends of God must, like clear verses, dispel doubts and drive away that unknown ignorant one through the power of proof.

order.why: Keep the sword imagery explicitly attached to speech.
Retain the forceful animal and flame metaphors within the regional instruction.
shortened: In any spot in the Caucasus, as soon as news arrives of these foolish ones, that soul must, like a piercing flame and striking lightning and swooping eagle, arrive and drive away that failing bat.

order.why: Keep the lion and flock imagery as the source’s own polemical language.
shortened: A few foxes have taken to prancing about in the field and plain, and several hyenas have fallen upon the sheep of God.

Since thou art a lion, thou must make an attack and show forth thy might, and drive away these weak animals so that the sheep and birds may burst into such melody in the gardens of the King of Manifestation as to astound the consciousness of the people of the world.

order.why: Read the injunction to the Hands of the Cause in its particular dispute.
Consider the hope for protection by the Hands of the Cause.
Read the fortress image and urgent call to vigilance.
shortened: Let them be a mighty fortress to defend His Faith, an impregnable citadel for the hosts of the Ancient Beauty. Let them faithfully guard the edifice of the Cause of God from every side; let them become the bright stars of His luminous skies. For the hordes of darkness are assailing this Cause from every direction, and the peoples of the earth are intent on extinguishing this evident Light. And since all the kindreds of the world are mounting their attack, how can our attention be diverted, even for a moment? Assuredly be cognizant of these things, be watchful, and guard the Cause of God.

order.why: Consider the sleeping guardian as an image of neglected responsibility.
Hear the concise plea for caution about a breach.
shortened: Great care and caution are needed so that no breach occurs in the mighty fortress of God's Cause.

order.why: Read the perceived stakes of protection in the source’s own terms.
shortened: The mighty fortress of God's Cause must be protected from the arrows of hatred and malice of such persons. Otherwise, the very foundation of God's religion will be completely destroyed.

order.why: Keep the hosts and fortress language within its religious setting.
shortened: Ye are God's hosts upon earth. Guard ye the fortress of My Cause from every doubting transgressor.

order.why: Retain the Pharaoh image as a call to vigilance.
shortened: It is incumbent upon you to strive to safeguard the Cause to the extent of your power, lest the Pharaohs prevail over the hosts of God.

order.why: Compare lamps, birds, roses, and lambs as images of vulnerability.
shortened: Iscariot must not be forgotten; the Divine sheep must constantly be guarded against devouring wolves; the light of the Cause of God must be protected from contrary winds by means of a glass chimney; the innocent birds must be shielded against the birds of prey; blooming roses should be saved from the outstretched hands of injustice; and the lambs of God must be fortified against the fierce and ravenous animals.

order.why: Read the nightingale-and-flower imagery alongside protection from deceit.
shortened: Therefore, O human nightingales, strive to know the Friend and cut off the autumn's transgressing hand from this flower of the All-Merciful's Paradise. That is, O friends of God, gird up firmly the loins of service and protect the people of the world from the deceit and hypocrisy of the people of discord.

order.why: Consider the garden’s need for guardianship.
shortened: But the guardians must protect that garden and meadow from autumn winds and preserve it safe and secure from the hands of thieves and transgression of neighbors.

order.why: Turn the image of protection inward toward divine love in the heart.
Read the related pearl image as a personal trust.
shortened: Guard thou the pearls of the love of God lest they be stolen by every rejected traitor.

order.why: Consider vigilance toward what is entrusted.
shortened: They must be vigilant at all times concerning the Trust of God, lest the treacherous seize and steal it.

order.why: Read steadfastness and righteousness as the named means of guarding that trust.
Keep the Bab’s counsel to Dayyan about protecting remembrance and knowledge.
shortened: We have answered that which thou didst mention in thy adorned Tablets, and We have made thee a king that thou mayest recount that which the eternal mirrors relate concerning Him Who is their Revealer, and that thou mayest be vigilant lest there cross thy mind that which would extinguish the fire of His heart, and that thou mayest be unto Him and unto that which He desireth to convey regarding the remembrance of God a beauteous protector. Guard thou it and thyself, that neither His knowledge nor thine own be encompassed by loss, and make ye mention of God's guides with beauteous remembrance.

order.why: Retain the direct personal statement of responsibility.
shortened: The protection of the Cause is incumbent upon thee.

order.why: Hear the practical purpose of preventing harm.
shortened: Convey greetings to all the loved ones, and exert utmost effort in protecting and preserving the Cause that no harm may occur.

order.why: Attribute the severe portrayal of opponents while reading its concern for the vulnerable.
Keep the instruction about access to particular places in its own setting.
shortened: It is necessary to prevent people from entering such places and to make every possible effort to protect the Cause from all directions, lest the satans make a breach.

order.why: Read the appeal to the divine name amid perceived danger.
Consider the community’s protection under the image of a shared tree.
shortened: When His Cause is protected, we all remain protected and preserved under the shade of His blessed Tree. Otherwise, alas for all from that great terror!

order.why: Explains unity as a protection against attempts to scatter the community.
Keep the reported assessment of surrounding peril attributed.
shortened: The blessed Cause is the Cause of God; yet from every side perils have encompassed it. All the peoples of the world have assailed the Cause. The meaning is this: from every direction danger hath encircled the blessed Cause.

order.why: Retain the reported fragment concerning responsibility for others’ injury and its omission.
Read the reported Constantinople story as a rhetorical anecdote.
Keep the reported distinction between essential and secondary proof within the particular question of marriage.
Read the reported argument about where to seek information as a claim inviting examination.
Hear the reported confidence in answering accusations.
Read the brief counsel to deny false rumors.
Connect taking responsibility with speech intended to attract.
shortened: Take thou the reins of the Cause with the power of thy Lord, then make mention of Him amongst the servants with such remembrances as will cause spirits to be attracted.

order.why: Read the Surih of the Temple’s image of protectors preserving beauty.
shortened: These souls are the protectors of the Cause of God on earth, who shall preserve its beauty from the obscuring dust of idle fancies and vain imaginings.  In the path of their Lord they shall not fear for their lives; rather will they sacrifice their all in their eagerness to behold the face of their Well-Beloved when once He hath appeared in this Name, the Almighty, the All-Powerful, the All-Glorious, the Most Holy.

order.why: Consider the Iqan’s paradox of attempted extinguishing intensifying a flame.
shortened: So much so that Pharaoh and his people finally arose and exerted their utmost endeavor to extinguish with the waters of falsehood and denial the fire of that sacred Tree, oblivious of the truth that no earthly water can quench the flame of divine wisdom, nor mortal blasts extinguish the lamp of everlasting dominion. Nay, rather, such water cannot but intensify the burning of the flame, and such blasts cannot but ensure the preservation of the lamp, were ye to observe with the eye of discernment, and walk in the way of God's holy will and pleasure.

order.why: Read the reported pruning analogy as an account of growth amid criticism.
shortened: The matter is now beyond their criticism and rebuke.

These refutations which are being launched out against the Cause are like unto the work of the gardener who lops off the lower branches of a tree and clears the ground from thorns and underbushes. This will cause the growth of the tree. Although outwardly the lopping of the branches may be considered as afflicting wounds to the tree, yet in reality, they will speed along its development.

order.why: Keep the supplied interpretation of Isaiah’s destructive instrument and its source omissions.
Read the Tablet to the Pope’s images of a message surviving suppression.
Hear the concise declaration of truth undiminished by force.
shortened: No force of hosts can weaken Him, nor can the might of kings enfeeble Him. He speaketh the truth and summoneth all unto the One, the All-Informed.

order.why: Read the stated readiness to recite before a world of opponents.
Consider justice and utterance confronting tyranny in the source’s testimony.
shortened: Before the faces of princes and divines, We have, with the pen of justice and utterance, struck at the swords of tyranny and rebellion, and We have been and continue to be like a brilliant and manifest light. Should the entire world unite and rise up to harm the Truth, it would be and is absolute nothingness. Verily, We fear no one.

order.why: Hear the prayer for preservation from distortion.
shortened: Therefore, O my God, protect it from the perversion of the extremists and the innovations of the innovators, and preserve the fortress of Thy Cause from those who would break away, through Thy power, O Thou Most Merciful of the merciful ones, and through Thy sovereignty which pervadeth the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.

order.why: Read the prayer for strength and an articulate tongue.
shortened: O Lord! Strengthen his back and gird up his loins and make his affairs easy and illumine his face and loose his tongue that he may make Thy servants firm in Thy Covenant and Testament and become a mighty barrier of iron between Thy servants and Gog of commotion and Magog of upheaval.

order.why: Close the linked selections with the hope of protection through grace.
shortened: This servant beseeches the Most Great Unity that you may be protected and preserved under the shadow of His grace - and this is not difficult for God.

order.why: Read the supplied assurance of an enduring foundation.
Consider the supplied warning about the need for scholarship and wisdom, preserving its omission.
End with impartiality, recognition of an opponent’s merits, and honesty about obligations.

questions: What does the forged-letter episode suggest about the relationship between careful evidence and the protection of people?
How might courtesy and the willingness to hear a doubt strengthen a reasoned response?
What responsibilities arise when one’s conduct is taken to represent a whole faith?
How does First Peter 3:15–17 connect explanation, conscience, and the way an answer is given?
What differences do you notice among general ethical principles, historical precautions, and accounts of particular controversies?
How could recognizing an opponent’s merits change both the substance and the purpose of religious argument?

references.label: 1 · 1 Peter 3:15–17 · Giving a reason with meekness
references.note: Read the King James Version’s connection between readiness to explain one’s hope, meekness, a good conscience, and conduct under accusation. Compare it with the compilation’s standards for courteous writing and impartial defense. Consider how the manner of an answer becomes part of its evidence.

subjects.displayTitle: Free will and fate: steering a life within conditions we did not choose
subjects.introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likens a human life to a ship: the wind or steam that drives it comes from beyond us, yet the rudder is in our hands. Sleep, sickness, loss and death are imposed, and no one is answerable for them; justice and injustice are chosen, and that choice belongs to no one else. God’s knowing what we will do is not the cause of our doing it, any more than a governor’s commission from the Sultan excuses his tyranny. Fate itself divides into the oil that must burn down and the gust that need not reach the flame, with prayer and prudence as a glass set around the lamp. The Qur’an invites each person to choose a path toward the Lord and at once grounds that choice in God’s will [1], and the Báb admits that reason alone cannot settle the matter. From here the inquiry turns to cause and effect and the necessary relationships that bind things, to the soul standing midway in creation, and to the mystery of suffering, which no account of choice explains away.
subjects.arc: Begin with the ship and rudder, distinguish knowledge from causation and choice from imposed conditions, then explore fate, prayer, moral growth, and the limits of explanation.

order.why: Open with the ship and rudder and the explicit limits of responsibility.
shortened: Certain matters are subject to the free will of man, such as acting with justice and fairness, or injustice and iniquity -- in other words, the choice of good or evil actions.

But there are certain matters where man is forced and compelled, such as sleep, death, sickness, failing powers, misfortune, and material loss: These are not subject to the will of man and he is not accountable for them, for he is compelled to endure them. But he is free in the choice of good and evil actions, and it is of his own accord that he performs them.

This condition can be likened to that of a ship that moves by the power of wind or steam. Should this power be cut off, the ship would become entirely unable to move. Nevertheless, in whatever direction the rudder is turned, the power of the steam propels the ship in that direction. If the rudder is turned to the east, the ship moves eastward, and if it is directed to the west, the ship moves west. This motion does not arise from the ship itself, but from the wind or steam.
In like manner, all the doings of man are sustained by the power of divine assistance, but the choice of good or evil belongs to him alone.

order.why: Keep the question about foreknowledge with the answer distinguishing knowledge from causation.
shortened: Question: When an action which someone will perform becomes the object of God's knowledge and is recorded in the "Guarded Tablet" of destiny, is it possible to resist it?

Answer: The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence; for the essential knowledge of God encompasses the realities of all things both before and after they come to exist, but it is not the cause of their existence.

order.why: Consider the governor’s responsibility for the use of delegated power.
Read the middle way as bestowed existence and creaturely action.
Compare a person’s chosen motion with a tree’s compelled motion.
shortened: Man's involvement in actions is through will, inclination, receptivity and capacity. Both man and tree are in motion, and God is the mover of both these motions. However, man's motion differs from the tree's motion, for the first is by choice, will and inclination, while the second is by compulsion and without choice, and the Mover is the Mighty, the Compelling One.

order.why: Distinguish sustaining power from the choice of how it is used.
shortened: However, this does not mean there is compulsion involved. Rather, it means that if sustenance were cut off, all created things would cease to move. For example, if the sustenance of the spirit were cut off from the organs and parts of the human body, no organ would retain any movement. However, this movement is according to the satisfaction and desire of the self, not the spirit.

order.why: Explore fate and predestination through necessary relationships and the active force of will.
Consider will and understanding in the Tablet to Forel.
Read discovery and craftsmanship as forms of human initiative within nature.
shortened: It is therefore evident that the natural movements of all created things are compelled, and that nothing moves of its own will save animals and, in particular, man.

Man is able to resist and oppose nature inasmuch as he discovers the natures of things and, by virtue of this discovery, has mastery over nature itself. Indeed, all the crafts that man has devised proceed from this discovery.

order.why: Keep the reported account of knowledge and command over nature in its own vocabulary.
Read the reported contrast between a creature’s environment and human invention.
Use the reported example of walking and building an aeroplane to distinguish conditions and possibilities.
Keep moral refinement distinct from the inability to stop aging or death.
Read effort and progress alongside humanity’s shared substance.
Consider purity at birth and the later acquisition of virtues or vices.
shortened: Know thou that every soul is fashioned after the nature of God, each being pure and holy at his birth. Afterwards, however, the individuals will vary according to what they acquire of virtues or vices in this world. Although all existent beings are in their very nature created in ranks or degrees, for capacities are various, nevertheless every individual is born holy and pure, and only thereafter may he become defiled.

order.why: Read divine measure beside the explicit role of one’s own volition.
Distinguish the Creator from the doers while retaining the source’s terminal omission.
Consider different uses of the same bestowed power.
Read the reported gap between knowing the good and acting under desire.
shortened: Some, let us suppose, know what action is good and what is bad, but at the time of action, self and desire prevail and they are overcome.

order.why: Consider the reported value of faithfulness that is freely chosen.
shortened: Real faithfulness is that kind which is volitional.
Therefore this free-will in man which God has created in man's being is the cause of adornment.

order.why: Read freely offered praise beside the compelled praise of other things.
Keep choice and individual capacity together in the report.
shortened: All souls have a free will to choose or refuse the Will of God.
Each soul has its station of individuality in which it may develop itself, but a soul cannot leave its own station for another station or individuality.

order.why: Hear the reported necessity of human participation in spiritual development.
Consider the reported possibility of accepting or rejecting divine guidance.
Read the Bab’s scriptural appeal to the absence of compulsion in religion.
Explore the stated purpose of allowing a response through one’s own powers.
shortened: He Who is the Dayspring of Truth is, no doubt, fully capable of rescuing from such remoteness wayward souls and of causing them to draw nigh unto His court and attain His Presence. “If God had pleased He had surely made all men one people.” His purpose, however, is to enable the pure in spirit and the detached in heart to ascend, by virtue of their own innate powers, unto the shores of the Most Great Ocean, that thereby they who seek the Beauty of the All-Glorious may be distinguished and separated from the wayward and perverse. Thus hath it been ordained by the all-glorious and resplendent Pen.

order.why: Read victory through speech as an opportunity for people to receive divine good.
Examine the four possibilities and the argument connecting justice, receptivity, and accountability.
shortened: For the matter resolves to one of four possibilities: either compelling all to obedience, or compelling all to disobedience, or compelling some to obedience and others to disobedience, or giving each its due according to the capacities of contingent beings.

Were we to assume compulsion in either obedience or disobedience, free will would be eliminated, and with its elimination obligation would be nullified, and with its nullification reward and punishment would fall outside the circle of righteousness. It befits not the Just and Wise One to bestow paradise on one who has not performed what merits it, or hell on one who has not done what warrants it.

order.why: Read the sun-and-rays analogy within the question about compulsion and mercy.
shortened: Therefore notice that the fact that rays are scattered from the sun to far and near does not mean that the sun has arranged some of them to be near and some of them to be distant but rather in bestowing existence it makes no distinction or augmentation with respect to any.  It has manifested all with the same effulgence.  But each, according to its own desire, has accepted a particular station and status.

order.why: Consider the Bab’s rejection of both compulsion and delegation.
shortened: In the perspective of Truth, it is neither predestination nor delegation. Rather, the Command of God transcends these two matters.

The secret of the Command is that God knows the volition of all things, and through the path of volition creates all things, and rewards them according to their volition. Were He to create anything contrary to its own degree of receptivity, He would have wronged it.

order.why: Read the Bab’s account of choice accompanying existence and divine action.
shortened: The servant, at the time of action, acts through the action of destiny from One All-Knowing and All-Wise, for God, glorified be He, has always known the choices of all and how they proceed therein, recompensing them according to their qualities and giving them their due.

This choice accompanies the existence of things, and nothing exists except through its choice, for at the time of the choice's existence when God the Exalted said "Am I not your Lord?", had there not been choice, the response "Yea" would not have been given.

order.why: Keep the distinction between willing what God loves and receiving existence through divine will.
shortened: Say: There is no volition except through God, and all act by His volition. Say: There is no will except through God; we stand through God. Say: If ye will what God loveth, then ye will through His will, and if ye will what God loveth not, then ye stand through His will.

order.why: Read decree and the servant’s choice together in the Bab’s technical vocabulary.
Consider an act’s irreversibility alongside the initial choice to perform it.
shortened: Consider thyself: thou performest an action of thine own free will, yet once done thou canst not reverse it. If thou shouldst act otherwise, would not the same hold true?

order.why: Read the refusal to blame fate for the wrongdoing of named historical figures.
Keep the Bab’s judgment concerning obedience and desire within its theological voice.
Read the report’s presentation of opposing philosophical positions without mistaking a quoted position for its final conclusion.
Explore the reported loom analogy as a distinction between given material and the manner of weaving.
shortened: Hear then, my children: the human soul is to be compared to a weaver, but human life to a woven fabric; the human body, and foremost the brain, is the implement, the organ, through which the weaving is done. God, the Lord, the taskmaster, covers the weaver's loom (the human milieu) with the warp of fate.

The human soul then weaves the weft of the fabric with the shuttle of the senses, the imagination and action until life's end, whereby - so we say -works of art of a human life appear. The material to be woven, be it hemp, yarn, wool or silk, or some other mixture, the soul cannot choose, nor the implement, but only the ways and means of weaving, insofar as they are not already predetermined to some extent by the material itself.

order.why: Consider the reported interdependence of the chain of creation.
Read the reported relation between events and connected parts.
Distinguish consequences of misconduct from conditions of the contingent world.
Consider the reported storm’s natural course and the vulnerability of a particular ship.
shortened: For example, a storm is a universal blessing. It is a prelude to cool and temperate weather. It is one of nature's features, an essential part of natural phenomena. However, if it strikes a ship which is incapable of resisting its force, this is not due to the ship's misfortune. The storm did not come to sink the ship but to follow its own natural course.

order.why: Keep the question about avoiding fate with the lamp’s conditional and irrevocable outcomes.
shortened: Question: Is fate, which is mentioned in the Holy Books, an irrevocable thing? If so, what use or benefit will come from seeking to avoid it?

Answer: Fate is of two kinds: one is irrevocable and the other is conditional, or, as it is said, impending. Irrevocable fate is that which cannot be changed or altered, while conditional fate is that which may or may not occur. Thus, the irrevocable fate for this lamp is that its oil will be burned and consumed.

But conditional fate may be likened to this: while some oil yet remains, a strong wind blows and extinguishes the lamp. This fate is conditional. It is expedient to avoid this fate, to guard oneself against it, and to be cautious and prudent.

order.why: Read the fuller lamp analogy and its account of protecting against contingent interruption.
shortened: Consider the lamp that is lit. Its irrevocable term is the exhaustion of its oil and wick, for as long as these two remain, the lamp continues to burn and give light. When these are exhausted, its extinction is inevitable and it will surely be extinguished.
However, it will attain this inevitable end only if the contingent terms that are created within existence by the power of the All-Merciful do not seize it and extinguish it first.

order.why: Consider prayer within the distinction between impending and irrevocable decree.
Read the limits of healing alongside prayer as a protective glass around a lamp.
shortened: For fate is of two kinds: suspended fate and irrevocable fate. Irrevocable fate cannot be changed or altered.
Rather, the purpose of seeking healing is to be protected from suspended fate and preserved from non-irrevocable destiny.

For example, consider that this lamp has a certain amount of oil, and when it burns and the oil is finished, it will certainly be extinguished - for this there is no change or alteration. However, benedictory prayers and seeking healing are like a glass that protects this lamp from opposing winds so that it is not extinguished by suspended fate.

order.why: Keep the reported distinction between a life’s term and a preventable death.
Retain the reported question about prayer and its answer concerning the lamp.
Hear the brief account of an ordained share for every atom.
shortened: For every atom among the atoms of contingent beings a portion hath been ordained and a share hath been established in the Book of God.

order.why: Read the scriptural reference to purpose and a fixed term in its source setting.
Consider the image of a leaf moving by divine will.
shortened: Praised be to Him and Exalted is He above everything that they ascribe as partner unto Him" [Q39:67]. Thus is it that not a leaf stirs upon a tree nor does a fruit fall except by the will of Thy Lord, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

order.why: Read the declaration that no combined power can prevent the divine will.
shortened: Even if all who are in the heavens and earth were to unite to prevent that which God hath willed, they would never be able, never have the power, and would find themselves utterly impotent.

order.why: Hold the Iqan’s invitation to choose beside its account of unanticipated divine destiny.
shortened: This is My counsel unto thee and unto the beloved of God. Whosoever wisheth, let him turn thereunto; whosoever wisheth, let him turn away.

For in Our solitude We were unaware of the harm or benefit, the health or ailment, of any soul. Alone, We communed with Our spirit, oblivious of the world and all that is therein. We knew not, however, that the mesh of divine destiny exceedeth the vastest of mortal conceptions, and the dart of His decree transcendeth the boldest of human designs. None can escape the snares He setteth, and no soul can find release except through submission to His will.

order.why: Consider trust in divine freedom as a source of steadiness.
Keep constancy rooted in the revealed word.
Hear the acknowledgment that destiny exceeds ordinary mastery of concepts.
shortened: This is a station wherein the feet of the mystics have slipped and the steps of the eloquent have stumbled. When one of the holy ones was asked about this most manifest station and this greatest vista, he replied that it was a surging ocean not to be entered, and in another instance, a pitch-dark night not to be traversed. He further said that destiny is a mystery among God's mysteries and a safeguard among His safeguards, sealed with God's seal, concealed within God's knowledge.

order.why: Read the related ocean-and-night imagery while retaining the quoted omission.
Consider the Bab’s invocation of a mystery between two extremes.
Keep the reported theological discussion and historical generalizations attributed, including its scriptural claim.
shortened: In truth, the Prophet Muhammad knew well that the difficult theological problem of the relationship of divine foreknowledge and conferment of grace to human free will is veiled in obscurity, as are also the mystery of suffering and the mystery of evil, of wickedness. For that reason the Prophet realized that this problem could easily become a stumbling-block for foolish and unlearned souls, and it is understandable that Muhammad did not like to hear in His presence idle disputations on this subject. Let us remember how the Prophet gave the clear instruction in the Qur'an: 'Do not sit together with someone who contends (quarrels) with fate, and do not start a conversation with such a one!'

order.why: Read the reported argument against meaninglessness and its distinctive rendering of the Hidden Words as a report.
shortened: The meaninglessness which appears to you in natural law, the inner and outer difficulties of the creature, will not trouble you, the word accident (the concept of meaninglessness) will help you to overcome the most difficult questions by burying them. - But if there is meaning behind all that happens, beyond cause and effect, then, so teaches us logic, there must be a meaningful Cause behind it all! There you have, O my son, caught the Godhead in the net of your logic!

The Blessed Perfection Baha'u'llah tells you about this in the Hidden Words (Arabic): 'Earthly calamity is My providence, My will, thy fate decreed by Me, in outward appearance it is purification, fire and punishment, in truth it is light and mercy, guidance and rescue. Why wilt thou flee from divine purification and guidance decreed for thee, as if it were meaninglessness (accident), aimlessness and purposelessness? Draw near to sorrow, accept suffering, embrace misery, so that thou mayest triumph as an eternal lamp and an immortal spirit.

order.why: Consider the devotional interpretation of affliction as bounty alongside the earlier limits of responsibility.
shortened: Whatsoever may happen is for the best, because affliction is but the essence of bounty, and sorrow and toil are mercy unalloyed, and anguish is peace of mind, and to make a sacrifice is to receive a gift, and whatsoever may come to pass hath issued from God's grace.

order.why: Allow the source’s acknowledgment of grief to stand beside its affirmation of wisdom.
shortened: Whatsoever hath come to pass is in conformity with wisdom, and all must needs be content therewith---nay rather, cherish hope in it. Yet in certain matters, when after the sweetness of reunion there cometh the bitterness of separation, and when after nearness and meeting the decree of remoteness is pronounced, it is for this reason that sighs of sorrow and grief are raised and the tears of the eyes are made to flow.

order.why: Read the reminder that a desired outcome need not be the best one.
shortened: O handmaiden of God! Be thou resigned unto fate and be satisfied with whatever the operation of destiny causeth to occur. Moreover, do not believe that whatever man desireth is also best for man.

order.why: Consider gratitude and acceptance in the face of what is ordained.
shortened: Therefore one must be content with fate and surrender to destiny, and be grateful and thankful for whatever has been ordained.

order.why: Discusses acceptance of destiny and contentment with divine decree.
Read the Bab’s counsel about contentment within the short duration of worldly life.
shortened: As for worldly affairs, in whatever age you live, dwell in the land with contentment and fear none but God, for the duration of this world compared to the life of the hereafter is less than a moment and shall pass. God has guaranteed the sustenance of His servants, and each shall receive what is destined.

order.why: Explore the chosen alignment of one’s will with divine purpose.
Distinguish fading one’s will in God’s will from identifying the two as equal.
shortened: Furthermore, no one's will hath ever been or shall ever be united with God's will, for the will of all hath been and shall ever be as nothingness before His will. The glory of existence is for one to make his own will fade away in God's will - that is, to have no will, thought or imagination of his own, but to move by God's will and act accordingly.

order.why: Read the reported appeal to Christ’s prayer of submission.
Consider the reported story of happiness through a transformed desire.
shortened: A man asked another: "In what station are you?" He answered: "In the utmost happiness." "Where does this happiness come from?" He answered: "Because all the existing things move according to my wish; therefore I do not find anything contrary to my desire; thus I have no sorrow. There is no doubt that all the beings move by the will of God, and I have given up my own will, desiring the will of God. Thus my will becomes the will of God, for there is nothing of myself. All are moving by His will, yet they are moving by my will. In this case, I am very happy."

order.why: Keep the reported image of guidance freeing a person from arbitrary impulses.
Read the reported distinction between capacity to act and desire to act in its account of the Prophets.
Attribute the report’s account of instinct and reward to its particular explanation.
shortened: The love shown by animals is instinctive and not dependent upon their own will--that is, they are endowed with their qualities and use them in a natural way, but not by their own will. As these qualities are instinctive and not voluntary, animals will not be rewarded. Their benefits are confined to this word only.

order.why: Keep the personal example of forbearance within the appeal to act according to divine will.
Hear the invitation to belief beside divine self-sufficiency.
shortened: Whoso willeth, let him believe in the signs of God, and whoso willeth, let him turn away. Verily, my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

order.why: Read the direct acknowledgment that counsel can be accepted or refused.
shortened: We counsel you for the sake of God - whoso wisheth, let him accept, and whoso wisheth, let him turn away.

order.why: Close the linked selections with the recipient’s freedom to respond to counsel.
shortened: This is the counsel of this servant. Whoso wishes, let him act upon it, and whoso wishes, let him turn away therefrom.

order.why: Read the supplied middle-way explanation through the ship’s power and steering.
shortened: Should the wind cease to blow, that is, if the assistance of God be withheld, the ship would be unable to move. It would neither move to the right nor to the left. But when the wind lendeth its assistance, the ship is set into motion. The inmates of the ship, however, steer it in whatever direction they please. Therefore the ship's motion, whether to the right or to the left, is generated through the assistance of the wind, and yet the sailors set the course of its movement. It is neither unconditional liberty for the ship saileth not through its own power, nor is it predestination, for the sailors of the ship steer it in whatever direction they please.

order.why: Retain this provisional rendering with its distinct wording and omissions.
shortened: If the wind bloweth not, that is if divine assistance be withdrawn, the ship cannot move. It can neither sail to the east nor to the west. But with the aid of the wind, the ship can be carried in whichever direction the rudder turneth. Thus the motion of the ship, either to the east or to the west, dependeth on the wind's assistance, but its course will follow the direction of the rudder, however it may be inclined. The words 'no deference,' signify that the ship cannot move by its own power whereas 'no compulsion' implieth that by means of its rudder, it is free to move in any direction. This is the meaning of the Middle Way.

order.why: Keep the second supplied rendering separate rather than silently merging it.
shortened: And yet, 'to all--both to these and those--will we prolong the gifts of thy Lord; for not to any shall the gifts of thy Lord be denied' If the wind bloweth not, that is if divine assistance be withdrawn, the ship cannot move. It can neither sail to the east nor to the west. But with the aid of the wind, the ship can be carried in whichever direction the rudder turneth. Thus the motion of the ship, either to the east or to the west, dependeth on the wind's assistance, but its course will follow the direction of the rudder, however it may be inclined. The words 'no deference,' signify that the ship cannot move by its own power whereas 'no compulsion' implieth that by means of its rudder, it is free to move in any direction. This is the meaning of the Middle Way.

order.why: Read the supplied distinction between sustaining assistance and foreordained action.
shortened: Should the aid of God be withheld from the world of being, no created thing would be able to move. It is not meant, however, that everything hath been foreordained, but rather that if the assistance of God be severed from the world, the entire creation would be bereft of the capacity to move.

order.why: Compare the supplied provisional account of human and tree motion.
shortened: The human being and the tree are both in motion and the mover for both is God. However, the movement of the human being is dissimilar from that of the tree for the movement of the former is based on choice, willpower and motivation and the movement of the latter is without volition or preference, and the mover is the Almighty, the All-Compelling. This is what is meant by 'neither by force, nor by deference, neither abhorrence, nor by command, but the middle way'.

order.why: Retain the provisional distinction between moral freedom and universal conditions.
Keep the machine-attributed provisional rendering and its claims about knowledge and nature distinct.
shortened: All universal beings and particular beings are firmly bound by the chains and fetters of nature, unable to transgress by an atom's weight - save human beings.

Humans have free will, nature is compelled. Humans have consciousness, nature lacks consciousness. Humans are living, nature lacks life. Humans discover future matters, nature is heedless of them. Through known premises, humans discover unknown conclusions, while nature is powerless to do so.

order.why: Read the supplied provisional account of universal relationships.
Consider the provisional candle analogy and its omission.
Keep the brief supplied fragment distinguishing two decrees.
Explore the supplied seven-stage account without erasing its technical terms.
shortened: "Nothing cometh into existence in the heavens or on the earth save through Will, Purpose, predestination, fate, permission, fixed-time, and the book." Every soul who entereth this world entereth with innumerable means, which although invisible to outward vision are true and fact. Whatever is irrevocably decreed by fate cannot be changed, but whatever remaineth potential can be changed through means and actions. The first inclination that is created in man, before the appearance of means, is the stage of the Will; the first conception of means is the stage of Purpose; predestination is the stage of scheme and dimension, that is to say, the appearance of means in proper quantity. Fate is the composition of that which hath been decreed.

order.why: Read the supplied provisional distinction between contingent limitations and divine will.
Keep the supplied provisional statement about inward divine will.
Consider the supplied account of why compelled acknowledgment lacks value.
shortened: Well is He able to search what lieth concealed in the hearts of men, and powerful is He to subdue the world and all that is therein by a word of His mouth. But were He to manifest such tokens, every man would either willingly or unwillingly acknowledge the truth of His Cause. Since such an acknowledgment is of no worth, the revelations of Divine power are, at one time, made manifest, while at another, they are withheld and concealed.

order.why: Read the Bab’s supplied provisional account of the limits of rational explanation.
shortened: Indeed, all who have endeavoured to explain the problem of Destiny have advocated either absolute divine determinism or human choice, and thus all the philosophers have confessed their powerlessness to explain the truth of this question. Indeed, this verily is the truth, inasmuch as the philosophers wanted to explain the divine truth, the Middle Path between absolute determinism and absolute freedom, by proofs of reason, which is, however, impossible.

order.why: Consider the supplied relation between free choice and the destiny-ordaining act.
shortened: Indeed, that free choice is bound to the existence of each thing, and naught is called into existence except through its free choice. Verily, at the primordial moment of choice, when God said unto the thing, "Am I not your Lord?" it would not have replied, "Yea," had it been deprived of freedom of choice.

order.why: Read the supplied account of distinctions appearing through choice.
Compare Ibn Arabi’s supplied account of decree and archetype while preserving its omission.
Read Melville’s weaving of chance, necessity, and will as a literary comparison.
End with the supplied invitation to choose a path toward the Lord.

questions: What does the ship’s rudder help you understand about freedom, and what questions does the analogy leave open?
How does distinguishing foreknowledge from causation affect the problem posed by the question in Some Answered Questions?
Why is the distinction between chosen conduct and unavoidable conditions important when judging oneself or another person?
What tensions or possibilities emerge when Qur’an 76:29 and 76:30 are read together?
How do the lamp and the weaver illuminate the relationship among precaution, prayer, circumstance, and action?
How might acknowledgment of mystery coexist with independent investigation and responsibility for one’s choices?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 76:29–30 · Choosing a path and depending on God
references.note: Read Pickthall’s translation of verse 29, then follow the adjacent verse 30. The invitation to choose a way toward the Lord is immediately followed by dependence on God’s will and knowledge. Compare the two verses together with the compilation’s distinction between the power that enables action and the direction freely chosen.

subjects.displayTitle: Material and spiritual civilization: what makes progress serve human life?
subjects.introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá never asked anyone to despise the lamp-glass. Material civilization, He says, is a means of progress, and He admired the commerce, industry and science He saw in Europe and America. His question is what the glass is for. Without the lamp of divine civilization inside it, the finest glass is dark; progress and barbarism, Bahá’u’lláh warns, walk hand in hand unless outward achievement is confirmed by character, mercy and the fear of God. The evidence lies in plain sight: one human family in which some members dress in costly garments while others go hungry, learning that can produce wisdom or deadlier weapons, wants that multiply with wealth, a culture that counts its monuments rather than the qualities of its people. Jesus told of a rich man who tore down his barns to build bigger ones on the night his soul was required of him [1], and the same reckoning hangs over every society that measures itself by what it has stored. To ask what makes progress serve human life is to begin weighing one’s own priorities. The path continues through the two kinds of civilization and the principle of balance and moderation, through the critique of Western values spoken in the voice of early twentieth-century visits, and through the heedlessness that any age can mistake for sophistication.
subjects.arc: Begin with the lamp and the unmet needs of one human family, explore moral direction and moderation, then read historical critiques of materialism before returning to renewal and purpose.

order.why: Open with the lamp-glass and the need to join material and divine civilization.
shortened: And among the teachings of Baha'u'llah is that although material civilization is one of the means for the progress of the world of mankind, yet until it becomes combined with Divine civilization, the desired result, which is the felicity of mankind, will not be attained.
Material civilization is like a lamp-glass. Divine civilization is the lamp itself and the glass without the light is dark.

order.why: Distinguishes material civilization from the spiritual refinement it requires.
Bring the question into the unequal conditions of one human family.
Read the reported contrast between elaborate pleasures and neglected poverty.
Consider cultivated morality as a test of outward civilization.
shortened: A superficial culture, unsupported by a cultivated morality, is as "a confused medley of dreams," and external lustre without inner perfection is "like a vapor in the desert which the thirsty dreameth to be water."

Be just: can this nominal civilization, unsupported by a genuine civilization of character, bring about the peace and well-being of the people or win the good pleasure of God? Does it not, rather, connote the destruction of man's estate and pull down the pillars of happiness and peace?

order.why: Read prosperity alongside the danger of progress joined to barbarism.
shortened: For although, on the one hand, material achievements and the development of the physical world produce prosperity, which exquisitely manifests its intended aims, on the other hand dangers, severe calamities and violent afflictions are imminent.

Progress and barbarism go hand in hand, unless material civilization be confirmed by Divine Guidance, by the revelations of the All-Merciful and by godly virtues, and be reinforced by spiritual conduct, by the ideals of the Kingdom and by the outpourings of the Realm of Might.

order.why: Keep the reported positive relation between moderated material progress and spiritual capacity.
Return to the lamp image as an account of the needs of the age.
Connect combined civilization with safety, comfort, and universal peace.
Read the reported relation between worldly prosperity and spiritual perfection.
Hear the report’s diagnosis of an imbalance between two kinds of progress.
Consider the reported measure of a country through its people’s qualities rather than monuments.
Read the reported ethical test applied to both religion and science.
Consider the reported gap between advocating peace and practicing it.
Read the reported counsel of moderation through ships, speed, and avoidable loss of life.
Hold scientific and industrial gains beside the proliferation of weapons.
Read the reported concern about improving instruments of violence.
Consider the reported contrast between armaments and moral comfort.
Keep the report’s concern that education can produce both wisdom and destructive skill.
Attribute the public address’s claim about aggression and material education.
Read the reported judgment concerning civil society amid violence in Tehran.
Keep the reported warning about an undiscovered force attributed without identifying a modern technology.
Read the reported question about technology with its extended answer and attributed predictions.
Keep the report’s severe account of the machine age and its heralds in historical context.
shortened: The material man far from God is, at best, a worshipper of humanity but, beyond that, a man of instincts who wants to take but not give, who strives ruthlessly for possessions, for power and means of power (money), who places the value of material goods and material pleasure above all else.

The age of technology, of the machine, of the material progress that promises happiness to all, has only just begun with the turn of the century (1900). The triumphal progress of technology is preceded by three heralds: materialism, atheism and mammon!

order.why: Consider the reported association of prestige with military preparedness.
Read the wartime report’s critique of patriotism and the effects of news of slaughter.
Consider the public address’s diagnosis of discord and absorption in possession.
shortened: Observe how darkness has overspread the world. In every corner of the earth there is strife, discord and warfare of some kind. Mankind is submerged in the sea of materialism and occupied with the affairs of this world. They have no thought beyond earthly possessions and manifest no desire save the passions of this fleeting, mortal existence.

order.why: Hear the concise warning that the language of civilization can accompany its destruction.
Read the reported growth of wants alongside accumulation.
Consider the reported sequence of escalating financial ambition.
shortened: From morning till evening, they run hither and thither, working and laboring, [sweating] and striving!  All their thoughts and ideals are weighed by the measures of Francs.  The man who has one hundred Francs does his utmost to make it a thousand.  The person who has one thousands works like a beaver to make it ten thousand.  The ten thousand man has his eyes fixed on a million; and the millionaire with the greatest avidity longs to become a multi-millionaire.  All of them are submerged in this sea of insatiable hunger for gold.

order.why: Keep the reported phrase dollarism as a critique of a governing priority.
Read the reported contrast between simple and complex lives in its historical vocabulary.
Consider the reported competing heralds of nationality, politics, commerce, science, and war.
Read the counsel neither to despair over poverty nor glory in prosperity.
shortened: Complain not from thy poverty neither glory in thy prosperity.  Be not sad from indigence in the means of thy livelihood, neither be thou disconsulate from lack of possessions.

order.why: Consider the impermanence of sovereignty and outward delight.
shortened: Although sovereignty tastes sweet to humans, ultimately disappointment, regret and remorse topple the foundation of joy and weaken the basis of delight. The earthly dust-heap becomes a dark grave, and the confines of the tomb become the dwelling of the prideful ones.

order.why: Read lofty buildings beside their eventual leveling.
Hear the reported limits of bodily progress and lasting satisfaction.
Keep the reported reflection after the loss of wealthy passengers at sea within its setting.
shortened: Look out upon this great city through which we are passing. Then think of the wealthy men entombed in the ocean's depths. The powers of man in material civilization are wonderful, but all his accomplishments are as nothing,--he, himself, is as non-existent unless he upbuilds in himself the civilization spiritual. Abdul-Baha has no other thought than this. This is his heart, his soul, his station, his service,--to quicken mankind with Divine breaths and walk in the pathway of the Heavenly Kingdom.

order.why: Consider the reported question of what produces a lasting result.
shortened: Europe has made extraordinary material progress, but if the qualities partake of the dust, what lasting result can accrue? The ideal to strive for is that which is in the supreme horizon - that is eternal! The underground is for worms and moles. That which is a cause for joy is a nest on the highest branch.

order.why: Read the public address’s appreciation of commerce and science beside its diagnosis of neglected spirituality.
shortened: When I came from the East and arrived in these lands, when I reached America, I observed that the nation had progressed greatly in material things - in commerce, in industry, and in material sciences.

However, I observed that spiritual progress had declined, that heavenly spiritual sensibilities had diminished, that attention to God had lessened, that all hearts were turned to worldly matters. Everyone desires to advance their physical life, acquire worldly wealth, and attain material comfort and ease. In brief, material sensibilities are abundant while heavenly sensibilities are few, and this is so throughout all regions of the world.

order.why: Keep the report’s judgment of Paris connected to its particular visit.
Read the public address’s encounter with Parisian scholars as an account of its own setting.
shortened: The evidences of material civilization there are very great, but the spiritual civilization is far behind. I found the people of that city submerged and drowning in a sea of materialism. Their conversations and discussions were limited to natural and physical phenomena, without mention of God. I was greatly astonished. Most of the scholars, professors and learned men proved to be materialists. I said to them, "I am surprised and astonished that men of such perceptive caliber and evident knowledge should still be captives of nature, not recognizing the self-evident Reality."

order.why: Retain the reported image of a spiritual sun below the horizon.
shortened: The darkness of materialism has enveloped Europe. Natural civilization has advanced tremendously and progress is magical and by leaps and bounds but the spiritual Sun with all its glorious lights is set below the horizon.

order.why: Consider the public address’s body-and-spirit image.
Keep the comparative judgment about countries attributed to the address.
